title: Thermodynamics and kinetics of a three-arm star polymer translocating through a nanopore
abstract: In this work, voltage-driven translocation of uniformly charged long linear and three-arm star polymers through narrow nanopores is investigated. Langevin dynamics simulation is performed using a coarse-grained model of the polymer and a semi-implicit representation of the nanopore. The mean translocation time of a linear polymer is found to be inversely proportional to the applied voltage over a wide range of voltages. In contrast, the mean translocation time of a three-arm star polymer of the same molecular weight exhibits a pronounced deviation from this scaling relation below a threshold voltage. The threshold voltage is found to be nearly independent of the molecular weight of the polymer but depends on the size of the nanopore and salt concentration. Metadynamics simulation is used to estimate the free energy landscape for the translocation of the three-arm star polymer. Below the threshold voltage, the free energy exhibits a pronounced second barrier resulting from an entropic contribution and electrostatic interactions between segments of the trailing arm inside the nanopore. A Fokker–Planck model developed using the estimated free energy accurately predicts the deviation from the scaling relation below the threshold voltage and shows a remarkable agreement with the Langevin dynamics simulation results using a voltage-independent fitting parameter. The agreement between the theory and the Langevin dynamics simulation results is seen for different nanopore radii, molecular weights of the polymer, and salt concentrations studied. A simple extension of the free energy landscape is suggested to predict translocation kinetics for higher molecular weights of the polymer without performing additional computationally expensive simulations.
relevance_reason: Coarse-grained Langevin dynamics plus metadynamics free-energy calculations for polymer nanopore translocation satisfy (a)-(c) as explicit-bead MD/enhanced sampling.

title: Modeling the inner electric double layer using short-range machine learning potentials: A critical assessment
abstract: Atomistic simulations of electrochemical interfaces typically require large system sizes and long simulation times to obtain reliable thermodynamic properties. In this context, machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) allow for computationally efficient sampling compared to density functional theory-based molecular dynamics simulations. Although conventional short-range MLIPs are recognized as inadequate for modeling the (potentially nanometer-wide) diffuse layer, they may still be capable of describing the inner electric double layer that is relevant for electrochemical reactions. Here, we evaluate the performance of common (short-ranged) MLIP architectures [the deep potential DP, the (graph) atomic cluster expansion-based models GRACE and MACE, and the pre-trained eSEN-OC25] for charged Au/electrolyte interfaces. In the evaluation, we focus on the effect of message passing and on the potentially adverse effect of data interference when training for a broad range of surface charges. Our results suggest that both local and message-passing models are able to reliably learn the interfacial structure when training on a single charge state. However, when trained on datasets that span multiple charge states, the MLIPs tested yield inconsistent predictions of interfacial water orientation and ion distributions. This behavior can be traced to the MLIPs being “blind” to the actual surface charge. Message-passing models show somewhat greater robustness to mixed-charge training data, likely due to their larger receptive field, but are still prone to artifacts and errors in the description of the interfacial structure. Overall, our results provide practical guidance on the expected accuracy and cross-charge-state transferability of short-ranged MLIPs for the description of the inner layer of electrode/electrolyte interfaces that will be relevant to their use in computational electrocatalysis.
relevance_reason: Systematic benchmarking of short-range MLIPs (DP, GRACE, MACE, eSEN-OC25) against DFT-MD for charged Au/electrolyte interfaces, i.e. MLIP development/benchmarking for atomistic simulation, satisfies (a)-(c).

title: Embedded atom method potentials for Si and Nb as alloying elements in Fe
abstract: Silicon (Si) and niobium (Nb) are chemical elements added to iron (Fe) alloys to improve their mechanical properties. In this work, we present a simple protocol for obtaining empirical interatomic potentials, based on the embedded atom method (EAM) formalism, for these alloying elements within the dilute limit (i.e. solute concentration typically below 1 at.%), using a potential already established for the matrix element, which was not refitted. The potential functions for Si and Nb were fitted to first-principles data where the alloying elements entered as substitutional impurities in the body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice of Fe. In addition to the distortion of the lattice caused by the insertion of Si or Nb, the interaction energies with point defects, such as vacancies and other Si or Nb atoms, were also included. Reasonable agreement was observed when comparing the results obtained with the EAM potentials with first-principles data not used in the fitting procedure (e.g. migration energies of Si and Nb by the vacancy mechanism). The new Fe–Si and Fe–Nb potentials are not intended to simulate the stable phases of the alloying elements individually, nor Si- and Nb-rich phases, such as the Fe2Si compound and the Fe2Nb Laves phase.
relevance_reason: Development and validation of embedded-atom-method (EAM) interatomic potentials for Fe-Si and Fe-Nb fitted to first-principles data directly satisfies (a), (b) classical force-field development, and (c).

title: External potentials for bottom-up coarse-graining of inhomogeneous fluids: On improving thermodynamic transferability
abstract: Bottom-up coarse-grained models derived from all-atom simulations of interfacial or strongly inhomogeneous molecular fluids often suffer from limited thermodynamic transferability due to insufficient sampling of composition variations in the reference simulations, which can bias learned interactions. Rather than increasing model complexity, we show that simple, pairwise coarse-grained models can achieve improved thermodynamic transferability when trained on reference ensembles with enhanced thermodynamic information. We introduce an external ensemble methodology that employs pairwise external potentials to drive equilibrium compositional fluctuations in the all-atom reference simulations of a model inhomogeneous dodecane–water system, thereby enriching the thermodynamic information available for coarse-graining. We show that this information content can be systematically quantified and optimized using a particle fluctuation number metric directly computable in the reference ensemble that is related to the Fisher information. Coupling this approach with relative entropy minimization, we show that maximizing the compositional fluctuations according to this information metric yields substantially improved coarse-grained model predictions of the all-atom alkane–water transfer free energies. We compare different coarse-graining protocols and types of external Gaussian potentials to show that this improvement is consistently observed. Finally, we show that improved alkane–water transfer free energies enhance predictions of hydrophobically driven self-assembly behavior, with external-ensemble-derived coarse-grained models yielding an order-of-magnitude improvement in the predicted critical micelle concentration of sodium dodecyl sulfate relative to conventionally derived coarse-grained models.
relevance_reason: Bottom-up coarse-graining of an inhomogeneous dodecane-water fluid trained on all-atom reference simulations with external biasing potentials and relative-entropy minimization — explicit atomistic-to-coarse-grained mapping, sampling methodology advance, satisfies (a)-(c).

title: Approximating committor functions: Objective functions and enhanced sampling
abstract: Many molecular dynamics simulations aim to study transitions between two states (from reactant to product states). In this context, the committor function (which gives, for a given molecular configuration, the probability of reaching the product state before the reactant state) is a pivotal quantity, in particular because it is the optimal importance function for rare-event simulation methods, such as importance sampling or splitting techniques. These methods are used to sample the reactive path ensemble and estimate, for example, the transition rate. However, learning such a function is generally a challenging task due to the high dimensionality of the configuration space. In this work, after reviewing existing methodologies to construct approximate committor functions, we propose a new loss function based on the application of Itō’s formula to learn the committor function with a minimization procedure on the parameters of a neural network. After comparing this novel approach to existing procedures on the Müller–Brown potential, we introduce a coupling strategy with the Adaptive Multilevel Splitting method to better approximate the committor function by improving the sampling of the reactive trajectories. This methodology, in which the committor function is iteratively learned, initially requires only knowledge of the reactant and product states.
relevance_reason: Enhanced-sampling methodology: neural-network committor learning with Itô-based loss coupled to Adaptive Multilevel Splitting for MD rare-event sampling — satisfies (b) and (c) as a free-energy/rare-event sampling method advance, though validation is on the Müller-Brown model potential.
